Rice.source_title: Integrated Pest Management Package for Rice (2014) - National Centre for Integrated Pest Management / DPPQS / NIPHM, Government of India

pests.name: Yellow stem borer
pests.symptoms: Larvae bore into the stem; causes 'dead heart' (dead central shoot) in the vegetative stage and 'whitehead' (empty, unfilled panicle) at the reproductive stage. National-significance pest — among the dozen insects of major economic importance on Indian rice.
pests.cultural_control: Clip seedling tips before transplanting to remove carried-over egg masses; use short-duration/short-stature resistant varieties (Ratna, Sasyasree, Vikas, HKR 46 and others); community-wide tillage and flooding of stubble after harvest to destroy diapausing larvae; adjust planting time to avoid peak moth emergence.
pests.biological_control: Release Trichogramma japonicum and T. chilonis egg parasitoids @ 1 lakh/ha on appearance of egg masses/moths; conserve natural predators (spiders, mirid bugs, carabid beetles, dragonflies); collect egg masses into bamboo cage-cum-perchers to allow parasitoid escape while trapping hatching larvae; pheromone traps @ 20 traps/ha (10-15 mg lure) for mass trapping of male moths from 20 days after transplanting.
pests.chemical_control: Nursery stage: Cartap hydrochloride 4% granules or Cartap hydrochloride 50% SP. Vegetative/panicle-initiation stage: Carbofuran 3% CG, Cartap hydrochloride 4% granules or 50% SP, or Monocrotophos 36% SL (as per NIPHM's crop-stage generic IPM module).
pests.dosage: Nursery: Cartap hydrochloride 4% granules @ 18750 g/ha or Cartap hydrochloride 50% SP @ 1000 g/ha. Vegetative & panicle-initiation-to-booting: Carbofuran 3% CG @ 25000-66600 g/ha, or Cartap hydrochloride 4% granules @ 18750-25000 g/ha, or Cartap hydrochloride 50% SP @ 1000 g/ha, or Monocrotophos 36% SL @ 625-1250 ml/ha.

pests.name: Brown planthopper / White-backed planthopper
pests.scientific_name: Nilaparvata lugens Stal / Sogatella furcifera Horvath
pests.symptoms: Sap-sucking insects clustering at the tiller base; causes 'hopper burn' — sudden yellowing and drying of patches in the field. National-significance pest; economic threshold 10-20 hoppers/hill depending on crop stage.
pests.cultural_control: Avoid excess nitrogen (promotes dense, susceptible canopy); alternate wetting and drying irrigation; drain fields 3-4 days during heavy infestation; grow no more than two crops per year with early-maturing varieties; use resistant varieties (Vijetha, Chaitanya, Krishnaveni and others).
pests.biological_control: Conserve natural predators — spiders (wolf spider Pardosa pseudoannulata, lynx spider Oxyopes javanus), mirid bugs, and other generalist predators; maintain a 2:1 pest-to-defender ratio threshold before spraying to avoid killing beneficials unnecessarily.
pests.chemical_control: Imidacloprid 70% WG, Imidacloprid 30.5% m/m SC, Ethofenprox 10% EC, Acephate 75% SP, or Buprofezin 25% SC, directed at the base of tillers where hoppers cluster.
pests.dosage: Imidacloprid 70% WG @ 30-35 g/ha, or Imidacloprid 30.5% m/m SC @ 60-75 ml/ha, or Ethofenprox 10% EC @ 500-750 ml/ha, or Acephate 75% SP @ 300-1000 g/ha (666-1000 g/ha vegetative, 300-500 g/ha at flowering), or Buprofezin 25% SC @ 800 ml/ha.

pests.name: Rice leaf folder
pests.symptoms: Larvae fold leaves longitudinally and feed on the green tissue within, leaving characteristic 'fully damaged leaves' (FDL) with a scraped, whitish, papery appearance. National-significance pest.
pests.cultural_control: Early planting to avoid greater leaf damage; wider spacing (22.5x20 cm or 30x20 cm) and moderate nitrogen use decreases damage; avoid over-fertilization (attracts females for egg-laying); remove shading within the field.
pests.biological_control: Conserve egg predators (crickets) from surrounding grass habitats; larval parasitoid Stenobracon nicevillei; egg parasitoid Trichogramma chilonis; pupal parasitoid Copidosomopsis nacoleiae.
pests.chemical_control: Cartap hydrochloride 4% granules or 50% SP, Monocrotophos 36% SL, or Chlorpyrifos 1.5% DP, at vegetative through panicle-initiation stages.
pests.dosage: Cartap hydrochloride 4% granules @ 18750-25000 g/ha, or Cartap hydrochloride 50% SP @ 1000 g/ha, or Monocrotophos 36% SL @ 625-1250 ml/ha, or Chlorpyrifos 1.5% DP @ 25000 g/ha.

pests.name: Gall midge
pests.symptoms: Larval feeding at the growing point produces a hollow, tubular 'silver shoot' gall in place of a normal leaf, and the affected tiller does not produce a panicle. Economic threshold: 1 gall/m2 or 10% silver shoot.
pests.cultural_control: Plough under ratoons of the previous crop; control grassy weeds/wild rice (alternate hosts) around the field; drain fields for 5-7 days; use early-maturing varieties and avoid staggered planting across a locality; use resistant varieties (Bhadrakali, Pavitra, Panchami and others).
pests.biological_control: Conserve general natural enemies of rice pests (spiders, carabids, coccinellids); maintain non-rice habitat refuges at field margins.
pests.chemical_control: Carbofuran 3% CG, Carbosulfan 6% G or 25% EC, or Fipronil 0.3% GR, applied in the nursery or at 20 days after transplanting.
pests.dosage: Nursery: Carbofuran 3% CG @ 25000-66600 g/ha, or Carbosulfan 6% G @ 16700 g/ha, or Carbosulfan 25% EC @ 800-1000 ml/ha. Vegetative (20 days after transplanting): Carbofuran 3% CG @ 25000-66600 g/ha or Fipronil 0.3% GR @ 16670-25000 g/ha.

pests.name: Rice hispa
pests.symptoms: Adults scrape the upper leaf surface leaving parallel whitish streaks; grubs mine within the leaf tissue producing blotch-like mines. Regional-significance pest (Bihar, West Bengal, Assam, Odisha, several other states).
pests.cultural_control: Clip and destroy the top three-fourths of heavily egg/grub-infested leaves at the early vegetative stage; sustained hand/sweep-net collection of adults; remove ratoons and volunteer rice in the crop-free season; skip nitrogen top-dressing during high hispa incidence.
pests.biological_control: Larval parasitoid Bracon sp.; conserve generalist predators active in the crop canopy.
pests.chemical_control: Quinalphos 25% gel or Chlorpyrifos 20% EC, sprayed at the vegetative stage.
pests.dosage: Quinalphos 25% gel @ 1000 ml/ha, or Chlorpyrifos 20% EC @ 1250 ml/ha.

pests.name: Rice caseworm
pests.symptoms: Larvae cut leaf pieces to build a floating case and feed on leaf tips, giving a ragged, cut appearance; more damaging in low-lying, water-logged fields in eastern India.
pests.cultural_control: Wider hill spacing (30x20 cm) reduces damage; early planting to escape peak moth activity; draining fields for 5-7 days kills larvae; older seedlings and optimal, split nitrogen dosing reduce abundance.
pests.biological_control: Conserve generalist aquatic and terrestrial predators in the paddy ecosystem (spiders, water bugs).
pests.chemical_control: Carbaryl 10% DP dust, applied at the vegetative stage.

pests.name: Termite
pests.symptoms: Attacks roots and stem base, mainly under moisture-stressed conditions; regionally significant in rainfed upland areas and irrigated rice-wheat systems, causing wilting and plant death in patches.
pests.cultural_control: Avoid moisture stress through timely irrigation; remove and destroy crop residue/stumps that harbour termite colonies.
pests.biological_control: Not specifically detailed in the source document for rice; general soil-borne-pest biocontrol practice is to conserve entomopathogenic fungi in undisturbed field margins.
pests.chemical_control: Seed treatment with chlorpyrifos 20% EC in termite-endemic areas.
pests.dosage: Chlorpyrifos 20% EC @ 10000 ml/ha as a seed treatment along with a 10% gum arabica solution, applied just before sowing; alternatively imidacloprid 200 SL (20%) @ 0.25 litre/100 kg seed with 10% gum arabica solution in 3.75 litre water.

diseases.name: Rice blast
diseases.symptoms: Diamond/spindle-shaped lesions with gray centers and brown borders on leaves; can also infect the panicle neck (neck blast), causing empty or partially filled grains. National-significance disease; economic threshold 3-5 lesions/leaf (early) or 2-5 neck-infected plants/m2 (panicle stage).
diseases.cultural_control: Use blast-resistant/moderately-resistant varieties (Rasi, Vikas, Krishna Hamsa, Tulasi, IR 64 and others); avoid excess nitrogen; seed treatment before sowing; balanced water management.
diseases.biological_control: Not detailed with a specific biocontrol agent in the source document for blast; general seed-treatment biocontrol (Trichoderma/Pseudomonas @ 5-10 g/kg seed) is recommended for soil/seed-borne fungal diseases generally.
diseases.chemical_control: Carbendazim 50% WP, Isoprothiolane 40% EC, Tricyclazole 75% WP or 70% WG, or Ediphenphos 50% EC at flowering.
diseases.dosage: Carbendazim 50% WP @ 250-500 g/ha, or Isoprothiolane 40% EC @ 750 ml/ha, or Tricyclazole 75% WP @ 300-400 g/ha or 70% WG @ 300 g/ha (nursery through panicle-initiation stages); at flowering, Ediphenphos 50% EC @ 500-600 ml/ha or Isoprothiolane 40% EC @ 750 ml/ha or Tricyclazole 75% WP @ 300-400 g/ha, with nitrogen kept to a small dose if needed.

diseases.name: Bacterial leaf blight
diseases.scientific_name: Xanthomonas campestris pv. oryzae (Ishiyama Swings et al.)
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked lesions starting at leaf tips/margins, turning yellow-white and drying out; a 'kresek' phase can wilt entire young seedlings. National-significance disease; ETL 2-3 infected leaves/m2 (or 2-3 plants/m2 in kresek phase at nursery).
diseases.cultural_control: Use resistant varieties (Ajaya, IR 36, IR 64, Swarna, Rajendra Basmati and others); avoid excess nitrogen and apply in more, smaller split doses; avoid clipping seedling leaf tips during transplanting; improve field drainage.
diseases.biological_control: Not detailed with a specific biocontrol agent in the source document; primary non-chemical management is resistant varieties and field/water sanitation.
diseases.chemical_control: Streptomycin sulphate 9% + Tetracycline hydrochloride 1% SP (nursery/vegetative stage); Streptocycline spray at early root stage, with a second spray before grain set if necessary.
diseases.dosage: Streptomycin sulphate 9% + Tetracycline hydrochloride 1% SP @ 100-150 ppm; Streptocycline 100-150 ppm solution, first spray at early root stage and second (if needed) before grain set, alongside reduced/split nitrogen application.

diseases.name: Sheath blight
diseases.symptoms: Oval, water-soaked lesions on the leaf sheath near the waterline that enlarge and merge, causing sheath and leaf drying; ETL is lesions of 5-6 mm length with 2-3 infected plants/m2.
diseases.cultural_control: 30 cm alley formations at every 2.5-3 m in sheath-blight-endemic areas to improve airflow; avoid excess nitrogen and dense planting; use tolerant varieties (PR 108, Bhudeb Dinesh, Jogan and others).
diseases.biological_control: Not detailed with a specific biocontrol agent in the source document for sheath blight.
diseases.chemical_control: Validamycin 3% L, Hexaconazole 5% EC, Propiconazole 25% EC, or Propiconazole 10.7% + Tricyclazole 34.2% SE.
diseases.dosage: Validamycin 3% L @ 2000 g/ha (or 200 g/ha at flowering, per the document's flowering-stage table) or 2000 ml/ha (panicle-initiation stage), or Hexaconazole 5% EC @ 1000 ml/ha, or Propiconazole 25% EC @ 750 ml/ha, or Propiconazole 10.7% + Tricyclazole 34.2% SE @ 500 ml/ha.

Rice.general_safety_precautions: The source document's Section 4 ('Safety Parameters in Pesticide Usage') directs extension functionaries to Annexure VIII (toxicity classification per the Insecticides Rules 1971 and WHO hazard classification, with the colour-coded toxicity triangle) and Annexure IX (basic precautions by toxicity/hazard class) before recommending any product, and stresses that farmers should be taught to read the colour-coded triangle on the product label, that first-aid measures for pesticide poisoning should be known to extension staff, and that product leaflets should be shared with local doctors ahead of spraying operations. Always use category-appropriate spray equipment (e.g. lever-operated knapsack sprayer with a hollow-cone nozzle at 35-40 psi for stationary/crawling pests; motorized knapsack/mist blower for airborne pests) per the document's application-technique protocol.
Rice.waiting_period_notes: The document does not tabulate a numeric pre-harvest interval (waiting period) per product for rice; it instead directs users to the WHO/Insecticides-Rules toxicity classification in Annexures VIII-IX and to the product's own label for safe-use timing. Always follow the specific pre-harvest interval printed on the purchased product's CIBRC-approved label.
